title: Precautions – abdominal
text: Rest, and take small sips of water. Eat light, plain food or nothing heavy until the pain settles. Note where the pain is and whether it is getting worse. Do not put a hot bottle on the belly if there is fever. the belly becomes hard or swollen, or the pain becomes unbearable there is blood in vomit, or black stool pain in pregnancy, or pain with fainting

title: Precautions – breathing
text: Sit upright and rest; loosen tight clothes. Stay away from smoke, dust and strong smells. Do not exert yourself until a doctor has checked you. they are breathless even at rest or cannot finish a sentence lips or nails look blue or grey chest pain, fainting or confusion starts

title: Precautions – chest_pain
text: Rest and avoid heavy work or exercise until a doctor has checked. Eat light meals and do not lie down right after eating. Keep someone with you and a phone within reach. the pain feels heavy or squeezing, or lasts more than 5 minutes the pain spreads to the arm, jaw or back, or comes with sweating, breathlessness or fainting

title: Precautions – cough
text: Drink warm water often; steam from a bowl of hot water may ease the throat (take care not to get burned). Cover the mouth when coughing and wash hands often. Stay away from smoke, dust and cooking fumes. they cough up more than a spoonful of blood they cannot speak in full sentences

title: Precautions – fever
text: Rest, and drink water, coconut water or soup often. Wipe the body with a cloth soaked in normal-temperature water; wear light clothes. Check the temperature with a thermometer every few hours and write it down. Use a mosquito net and keep standing water away from the house. the neck becomes stiff or a purple rash appears that does not fade on pressing there is bleeding from gums or nose, black stool, or vomiting blood they have a fit (seizure)

title: Precautions – headache
text: Rest in a quiet, dim room and drink water. If dizzy, sit or lie down at once and stand up slowly. Eat regular meals and avoid long screen time. Do not drive while dizzy or after fainting. a sudden, worst-ever headache starts the face droops, an arm or leg becomes weak, or speech becomes difficult they faint again, or have a fit

title: Precautions – urinary
text: Drink enough water through the day, unless a doctor has told you to limit fluids. Do not hold urine for long; keep the area clean and dry. Note the colour of the urine and any fever. they cannot pass urine at all, with a painful swollen lower belly high fever with shivering, back pain and vomiting they become confused or very drowsy

title: Precautions – vomiting
text: Give small sips of fluid often: water, rice water, coconut water or dal water. Keep giving breast milk or normal feeds to babies. Wash hands with soap after the toilet and before food; drink clean or boiled water. Watch how often urine is passed. they cannot keep any fluid down, or pass no urine for 12 hours (8 hours in a child) there is blood in vomit, or black stool they become very drowsy or confused

title: Clinical pathways spec – 0.1 Complaint-based, like real triage
text: Real triage starts from the chief complaint, not from a disease. We implement 5 deep pathways: | # | Pathway | Covers (internal concern patterns) | |---|---|---| | 1 | **Fever** (bukhar) | viral, dengue-like, malaria-like, typhoid-like, jaundice/hepatitis-like, chikungunya-like, urinary infection-like, meningitis-like, pneumonia-like | | 2 | **Cough** (khansi) | dry, wet/productive, blood in cough, asthma flare, pneumonia-like, TB-like (>= 2 weeks) | | 3 | **Stomach** (ulti / dast / pet dard) | gastroenteritis, dehydration, dysentery, GI bleeding, appendicitis-like, obstruction-like | | 4 | **Chest pain** (seene mein dard) | heart-like, acidity-like, muscle/chest-wall, breathing-related | | 5 | **Headache** (sir dard) | tension/migraine, fever-related, stroke-like, meningitis-like, head injury, high BP, pregnancy-related | A message can trigger more than one pathway (for example fever + cough). Run all matching pathways; the **final urgency is the most urgent** across them, and the care type comes from the most severe one.

title: Clinical pathways spec – 0.2 Severity stages (same ladder for every pathway)
text: | Stage | Meaning | Typical routing | |---|---|---| | **S0** Mild | Self-limiting, no warning signs | `gp_teleconsult` · `routine` | | **S1** Needs assessment | Needs vitals/tests or a doctor today | `paramedic_home_visit` or `gp_teleconsult` · `same_day` | | **S2** Warning signs | Could get worse quickly; needs a doctor/specialist or nursing care today | `gp_teleconsult` / `specialist_referral` / `nurse_home_visit` · `same_day` (some `immediate`) | | **S3** Emergency | Danger signs | `emergency_referral` · `immediate` (skip matching, show call-for-help) |

title: Clinical pathways spec – 0.3 Ask like a senior doctor, but stay within 4 questions
text: A senior doctor asks in this order: **danger signs first → onset and duration → character → associated symptoms → who the patient is (risk factors) → reports**. To stay within the 4-question limit: - Use **multi-select chips**. One tap answers many slots ("Inme se kya-kya hai?"). - **Skip** any question whose slots are already in the user's text. - **Stop immediately** when an S3 sign appears. Never ask further questions on an emergency. - Always include a "Kuch nahi / None of these" chip.

title: Clinical pathways spec – 0.4 Numbers we must extract (slot parser)
text: | Slot | Formats to handle | |---|---| | Temperature | `103`, `103 F`, `103°`, `39.5`, `39.5 C`, "tez bukhar", "bahut tez" (no number → ask). Values 35–43 → °C; 95–110 → °F | | Duration | "2 din", "do din", "parso se", "kal raat se", "ek hafta", "3 hafte", "mahine bhar se", "since Monday" | | Age | "6 mahine ka baccha", "2 saal", "75 saal ke papa", "buzurg", "newborn", "infant" | | Platelets | "40000", "40,000", "40k", "40 hazaar", "0.4 lakh", "1.2 lakh", "40 thousand" | | BP | "180/110", "BP 160 by 100", "BP high hai" (no number → ask if relevant) | | Counts | "5 baar ulti", "8-10 baar dast", "din mein 6 baar" | | Blood amount | "dhaage jaisa / thoda sa" vs "chammach bhar / bahut / baar-baar" |

title: Clinical pathways spec – 0.5 Risk modifiers (apply across all pathways)
text: | Modifier | Rule | |---|---| | Infant < 3 months with fever >= 100.4°F (38°C) | **S3** | | Child < 5 with any general danger sign: cannot drink/breastfeed, vomits everything, convulsion, very sleepy/unconscious | **S3** | | Elderly 65+ | Raise fever, cough and stomach pathways by one stage (max S3). New confusion → **S3** | | Pregnancy | Fever → at least S1 `same_day`. Abdominal pain, bleeding, or headache with vision changes/swelling → **S3** | | Diabetes, heart, kidney or liver disease, cancer/chemo, on steroids, HIV | Raise by one stage | | Bedridden / cannot travel | Prefer a home visit over teleconsult at the same urgency | ---

title: Clinical pathways spec – 7. Combining with the ML models
text: - Pathways are deterministic rules that produce `{stage, care_type, urgency, triggered_signs, concern_patterns}`. - ML ensemble predictions are still computed. - **Final urgency = the most urgent of (pathway, ML)**. Care type: the pathway's when its stage was decided by explicit rules; otherwise the ML ensemble. - The safety gate still runs first and last; S3 from any pathway = emergency path. - For the hidden test (single message, no follow-ups), pathways work on whatever slots are present; missing slots never lower urgency.

title: Clinical pathways spec – 8. References (for the write-up; verify exact editions before citing)
text: - WHO, *Dengue: Guidelines for Diagnosis, Treatment, Prevention and Control* (2009): warning signs and severe dengue criteria. - National Center for Vector Borne Diseases Control (NCVBDC), India: dengue, malaria and chikungunya guidance. - WHO, *Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI)*: general danger signs in children. - NICE NG143, *Fever in under 5s*: traffic-light system for children. - National TB Elimination Programme (NTEP), India: cough of 2 weeks or more as presumptive TB. - Standard emergency chest pain and stroke (FAST) red flags.

title: Symptom categories – CATEGORY 1 — COUGH AND SPUTUM
text: Initial choices: - Dry cough. - Wet cough or cough with mucus. - Wheezing or chest tightness with cough. - Cough with blood in sputum. - Persistent or recurring cough. Relevant follow-up questions may cover: - Duration and onset. - Whether symptoms are worsening. - Mucus characteristics where useful. - Fever or chills. - Breathlessness. - Chest pain. - Wheezing. - Night sweats. - Unintentional weight loss. - Relevant TB exposure or contact when appropriate. - Other relevant medical risk factors. Possible educational explanations may include airway irritation, allergies, respiratory infections, bronchitis, asthma-related problems, pneumonia, tuberculosis, and other causes when supported by the reported information. Do not automatically conclude that cough with blood means tuberculosis. Blood in sputum must trigger additional safety assessment and appropriate medical evaluation. A few small streaks and substantial bleeding must not receive identical handling. If blood is accompanied by severe breathing difficulty, chest or upper-back pain, fainting, or other documented emergency warning signs, show emergency guidance immediately. Persistent cough with relevant TB-associated symptoms should trigger appropriate professional evaluation and guidance about formal testing. Never diagnose TB from symptoms alone.

title: Symptom categories – CATEGORY 2 — FEVER AND CHILLS
text: Ask relevant questions about: - Duration. - Measured temperature, if available. - Chills and general condition. - Associated cough or breathing symptoms. - Rash. - Headache or neck stiffness. - Vomiting or inability to drink. - Confusion or unusual drowsiness. - Relevant exposures and risk factors. Explain possible infectious or non-infectious causes cautiously. Emergency warning signs must be checked before continuing ordinary questioning. Do not infer fever severity when the user has not measured or reported a temperature.

title: Symptom categories – CATEGORY 3 — BREATHING PROBLEMS
text: Ask about: - Sudden versus gradual onset. - Difficulty breathing at rest. - Ability to speak normally. - Wheezing. - Chest pain. - Blue or grey lips. - Fainting or confusion. - Relevant history when necessary. Severe or sudden breathing difficulty and other established emergency warning signs must trigger immediate escalation. Do not continue a lengthy AI interview while an emergency response is indicated. Do not reassure a breathless user that the problem is merely anxiety or allergy without adequate evaluation.

title: Symptom categories – CATEGORY 4 — CHEST PAIN
text: Ask relevant questions about: - Location and onset. - Nature of the pain. - Duration. - Whether the pain spreads elsewhere. - Breathlessness. - Sweating, fainting, nausea, or other associated symptoms. - Relevant medical history. Emergency warning signs must be evaluated immediately. Do not use a chatbot to rule out a heart attack or another serious cause. Possible explanations must remain educational and secondary to appropriate safety guidance.

title: Symptom categories – CATEGORY 5 — HEADACHE AND DIZZINESS
text: Ask about: - Sudden versus gradual onset. - Severity and progression. - Vision or speech changes. - Weakness, numbness, confusion, or fainting. - Fever and neck stiffness. - Recent head injury. - Relevant medical history. Severe sudden headache, new neurological symptoms, significant injury, or other documented warning signs must trigger appropriate urgent or emergency guidance. Possible explanations may include migraine, tension-type headache, dehydration-related concerns, and other causes where appropriate. Do not diagnose stroke, migraine, or another neurological condition from a conversational model alone.

title: Symptom categories – CATEGORY 6 — ABDOMINAL PAIN
text: Ask about: - Location. - Onset and duration. - Severity and progression. - Vomiting. - Fever. - Abdominal swelling. - Blood in vomit or stool. - Urinary symptoms. - Relevant pregnancy possibility where appropriate and voluntarily disclosed. Escalate concerning patterns using documented safety rules. Do not automatically label abdominal pain as acidity or indigestion.

title: Symptom categories – CATEGORY 7 — VOMITING AND DIARRHEA
text: Ask about: - Duration and frequency. - Ability to keep fluids down. - Signs that may suggest dehydration. - Urine output changes. - Blood in stool or vomit. - Fever. - Severe abdominal pain. - Relevant vulnerability factors. Provide general educational guidance when appropriate. Identify warning signs that require medical evaluation. Do not prescribe medication or invent dosage instructions.

title: Symptom categories – CATEGORY 8 — URINARY PROBLEMS
text: Ask about: - Pain or burning during urination. - Urination frequency. - Visible blood. - Fever or chills. - Back or flank pain. - Vomiting. - Difficulty passing urine. - Relevant pregnancy status or medical history when necessary. Explain possible urinary or kidney-related causes cautiously. Use documented warning signs to determine the appropriate escalation path.

title: Symptom categories – Objectives
text: 1. Identify the user's primary symptom category. 2. Ask relevant follow-up questions based on each answer. 3. Maintain an accurate temporary assessment state. 4. Detect missing, contradictory, unclear, and potentially serious information. 5. Identify relevant possible causes without claiming a confirmed diagnosis. 6. Evaluate urgency using deterministic safety rules. 7. Explain why an urgency category was selected. 8. Recommend safe next steps. 9. Offer suitable public-resource discovery, nearby hospital search, or caregiver matching where appropriate. 10. Offer an authorized emergency-contact action when warranted. 11. Preserve the user's privacy and never invent successful external actions. 12. Monitor application behavior and assessment quality without unnecessarily storing sensitive health information.

title: Symptom categories – The eight primary symptom categories
text: Implement eight complete assessment workflows. Each category must have its own relevant follow-up logic, safety checks, missing-information handling, possible-cause explanations, and appropriate next actions.
